Present-day models tend to produce code that is too defensive, too complex, too local in its reasoning. They avoid strong invariants. They add fallbacks instead of making bad states impossible. They duplicate code, invent bad abstractions, and paper over unclear design with more machinery.

comments.author: wrs
comments.text:
Aside from this lack of “big picture” stuff, I found Opus 4.7 had a strong tendency to explicitly decide to take shortcuts or defer known issues. Often it would even unilaterally cancel part of the agreed implementation plan, and hide that decision in the “thinking” (which is now off by default in Claude Code…turn it back on!). Its usual justification was that we needed to “deliver value earlier”. This has has improved in 4.8.

In any case, it reinforces that these full-auto loops just don’t work for most interesting tasks. If you’re not doing something low-level with direct automated feedback (like porting existing code with existing tests), human judgment is still needed frequently to keep things on track.

comments.author: thombles
comments.text:
If in doubt, add more AI. :) e.g. from https://lobste.rs/s/goo5sh/making_budget_models_punch_above_their


Finally, the loop doesn’t just take the model’s word that it has finished. A pre-finalization gate checks whether the code was changed and whether a build or test ran and passed. If not, it injects a soft nudge to get the model to actually finish specified tasks. When you set up a critic_provider, substantive runs escalate to a bounded second opinion. This judge asks: is this really complete and correct? If not, the run goes back into the loop for more work.

comments.author: zupzup
comments.text:
Security is the clearest example today. Even if you do not use loops to build your software, other people will use loops against your software.


It's almost as if Anthropic's messaging for the last months was aimed at creating exactly this feeling in people.

"Oh no, our models are too powerful and will find all the vulnerabilities! Luckily, our products help you guard against this - start today at 30% off with code DARIOHASYOURBACK!"

How well this worked can be seen in the certainty in which the article frames this unavoidable future:


If attackers and reporters loop, defenders will eventually need to loop too to keep up.


As with many articles about these topics, there seems to be a lack of at least a healthy amount of skepticism towards the quoted people who tout this new, unavoidable way of doing things (which coincidentally uses the maximum amount of tokens possible and creates the maximum amount of dependency on the products - curious!) and some critical self-reflection whether one simply fell for another round of AI propaganda.

comments.author: zetashift
comments.text:
I find that past weeks I've been really torn about what "technical value" means, for me but also what it means for small/large groups of people, especially as my interactions with LLM fanatics almost ends up feeling like I just got a peek into a cult.

When it comes to software I use weekly, they have been wasting more of my time(so many popups/updates/weird bugs!), and more importantly my attention, than before the slop. I've seen cool examples where a LLM helped out a person, so I don't think it's all bad. But because of this I share most of the concerns expressed in the post(even though I disagree in certain other parts).

But more importantly, as an unimportant software developer, why would I want to have so many layers so much of the time?

Like what is the ratio of reasons loops are working astonishingly well in certain domains:


because its inherent technical value is so good.

because it's novel and makes people feel like the manager they never could be.

because it's an amazing rubberduck

some other non-technical reason.


I just can't see a scenario where somebody so far away from the process (even if there is technical value there), would make me care for their FOSS project. I do this frequently now as well: if the README is slopped good chance I'm closing that browser tab.

comments.author: mitsuhiko
comments.text:
I find that past weeks I've been really torn about what "technical value" means, for me but also what it means for small/large groups of people, especially as my interactions with LLM fanatics almost ends up feeling like I just got a peek into a cult.


I know this trope is overplayed but the "no great genius has existed without a strain of madness" quote comes to mind when engaging with folks who are excessively trying all of this today. A lot of what is going on really looks mental and like performative art on the outside, but yet when you truly talk to the people who are doing the loop thing, many of them are way more rational than you would think. There is a lot of exploration going on in that space that is though provoking.

Spend some time in the issue tracker of Bun to see what I mean. It looks absolutely bonkers to me, and yet that is seemingly how that project runs now and … it sort of works? At least it's not nearly as broken and bad as one would imagine.

comments.author: zetashift
comments.text:
I'm all for experimentation, and as somebody who hopes niches like Unison and Gleam get more popular, I'm also empathic to the view that it all looks like mad talk(queue meme of Charlie Day looking crazy) from the outside.

But the provoking thoughts that come to mind when it comes to these hands off approach specifically is, at what point is this sheer momentum/luck/optics/whatever-you-call-it rather than inherently valuable necessary tech? Why would I invest my time and attention in using such a thing that's so vibecoded? Because somebody says its not vibecoded, it's looped agents calling each other?

I haven't looked at Bun in such a long time, because when 1.0 got launched(I was using it when it was 0.7), I still had so many papercuts with it. So when the Zig->Rust thing came up, my initial thought was "so Deno's technical choices do make sense". Yet still Bun probably inspires more awe/hype than Deno. It's not an unique case, but it does feel overwhelming to see it happen at such a scale, to the point that people might use something technically less suitable because LLMs work better with it.

Basically I can very well imagine Bun being a working engine, but is that because that rewrite had astonishingly good usage of LLMs, or because well...it's associated with one of the most relevant companies right now, and beforehand already had a lot of people's buy-in, because who the BDFL is?

(yes it's probably more nuanced, that's where all the torn feelings are coming from).

Another example: I'm not against cloud providers like AWS and GCloud, but I also wouldn't recommend certain classes of tech companies to be entirely dependent on it. And while people can discuss the technical values in cloud computing, people are still going with the wave. It feels like we can learn a lot from past trappings in tech, but people it doesn't seem like that is happening. At least for me, if I look at the sheer amount of people around me that interact with a LLM(socially and technically).

comments.author: travisgriggs
comments.text:
This may be one of the most resonant posts I've seen on this subject and my own reaction to it. I find myself curious how similar the author and I are in age/experience. Especially this paragraph in particular:


Part of that is taste and part of it is control. I attempt to set a high bar for what I want code to look like, and I want to understand the code I ship. Under pressure, or in a discussion with another human, I want to be able to explain what the system does without first having to ask a clanker to explain it to me. Now there is obviously a question if this desire to understand the code is one that I will still have a few years from now. For now I have not moved past the point of comprehension being important to me.


A few days ago, when Fable was available, I decided to have it write a chunk of C code for me. We do updates of firmware over BLE. And I wanted to entertain a wire protocol variant. The device has a wire protocol already, so it's really just abstracting out the upgrade engine so it could be driven by either BLE or the wire engine, and then adding the commands/events to the wire protocol. Fable did a decent job. I had to steer it a couple of times and, as the author points out, tell it not to stress about certain conditions that I know from external context are just not possible. It was about 2.5 hours of bot-sitting. About $40 of tokens. It was kind of boring. I prompted, played BZFlag until I heard the "done" beep, checked in, adjusted, then shot more tanks. My big misgiving at the end was that I did not "know" the code. Not that I remember every bit of code I've ever written, but often when visiting old code, it's like reacquainting with an old friend. And in this case, that just wasn't the case. I could do some test runs, and I'm reasonably sure it would work. But there is a discovery process when writing code, where as you're expressing the algorithm, your brain sees "ah, there's an edge/corner case here, I need to wrestle with whether to worry about that and if it is a concern, how to mitigate". Without doing the journey myself, I could not feel comfortable that the decently written code was really what I wanted in all cases, not just the happy paths.

So I wrote the code myself. Took 2 hours tops with Zed's very useful autocomplete. I was happier with the code I wrote. I knew it. And then I asked Claude to take a look at it. It sycophantically commended my work and pointed out "used the wrong variable here" (which both had the same type, so yay for type safety, eh?). I was much happier with this model. It cost the company less.

comments.author: wrs
comments.text: One of the unsung modes of using LLMs is the ability to explore the design space cheaply. Instead of just thinking about alternatives, you can have an LLM actually implement the alternatives and see where they take you. Once you settle on an approach, you can then delete it all and write it yourself, with a pretty cheaply bought confidence that you’re doing it the right way.
